claims.text: Variations in composition within the FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni family modify stacking fault energy.
Stacking fault energy alters the propensity for deformation twinning.
Differences in deformation twinning govern differences in strength and ductility among these alloys.
The thermomechanically processed equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline is single-phase FCC.
Using identical thermomechanical treatments and deformation conditions will provide comparable initial microstructures across the alloys.
The density, spacing, and distribution of mechanically induced twins are controlled by effective stacking fault energy.
Lower stacking fault energy promotes nucleation and growth of deformation twins during loading.
Deformation twins act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Twin-induced obstruction of dislocation motion enhances strain hardening and strength.
Relatively high stacking fault energy suppresses deformation twinning and favors dislocation-slip-dominated deformation.
Compared with the equiatomic quinary baseline, lower-stacking-fault-energy compositions will develop a higher density of deformation twins.
Compared with the baseline, lower-stacking-fault-energy compositions will exhibit increased yield strength.
Compared with the baseline, lower-stacking-fault-energy compositions will exhibit a steeper work-hardening rate.
Higher-stacking-fault-energy subsets will show less twinning and smaller twin-related strengthening contributions.
Higher-stacking-fault-energy subsets may undergo localized deformation earlier.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-family alloys produced through comparable thermomechanical processing paths.
